title: Monte Carlo Experiments of Network Effects in Randomized Controlled Trials
extended_summary:
This paper examines how randomized controlled trials can be distorted when the units being studied are connected in a social network rather than independent of one another. The central question is how network structure creates spillover, dampening, clustering, and related effects that bias treatment-versus-control comparisons. The author argues that conventional RCT assumptions break down in networked settings such as online social platforms.

The approach is not a human-subject educational intervention but a set of Monte Carlo simulations run on Watts-Strogatz random graphs. Nodes represent users producing content over time, with each node’s output influenced both by its own intrinsic production rate and by neighbors’ prior output. The paper simulates synthetic treatment assignment and quantifies effects such as spillover into control, experiment dampening, intrinsic dampening, degree distribution effects, clustering effects, and experiment size effects.

There is no student, teacher, school, or classroom sample in this study. The population is an abstract network of simulated nodes/users, motivated by online social networks such as Facebook or Twitter/X rather than educational contexts. The treatment and control groups are simulated subsets of graph nodes, not real participants, and no writing, motivation, or ChatGPT-related outcomes are measured.

The main conclusion is that in networked environments, standard treatment-versus-control estimates can systematically underestimate the true treatment effect because treated units influence controls through the network. The author recommends modeling the underlying graph structure and using simulation-based baselines when interpreting experiments on social networks. For the retrieval purpose described here, this paper is not the alleged 2026 high-school ChatGPT writing RCT and should be excluded from any quantitative synthesis of ChatGPT-based writing feedback in secondary education because it contains no educational intervention, no writing outcomes, no motivation outcomes, and no human participants.
quality_tier_rationale: This is an arXiv methodological simulation paper about network effects in randomized controlled trials, not an educational intervention study. It contains no student sample, no ChatGPT use, no writing or motivation outcomes, and no empirical education design to appraise under the K-12 intervention evidence framework.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports no educational outcome impacts because it does not evaluate an education technology intervention or learner outcomes. Therefore it provides no usable impact estimate for quantitative synthesis on ChatGPT-based writing feedback in high school.
